name: Nocamán
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

earlier_scan.source_named: Extinct; Glottolog entry retired (merged into Cashibo-Cacataibo 2023). Only Tessmann 1930 wordlist material known; no phonological description located.

new_statements.quote: The metrical system is trochaic, that is, feet are left-headed. These trochaic feet are created from left to right (i.e. from the beginning to the end of words). Generally, metrical feet in Kashibo-Kakataibo have to be disyllabic and degenerate feet are only admitted under very specific circumstances (see §4.3.6). In addition, the position of the primary stress (manifested as vowel lengthening) follows a different principle for predicates and non-predicates. Predicates carry the primary stress on the head of the rightmost (i.e. last) foot. Non-predicates carry the primary stress on the head of the leftmost (i.e. first) foot.
new_statements.citation: Zariquiey Biondi, Roberto. 2011. A grammar of Kashibo-Kakataibo. PhD thesis, La Trobe University, Bundoora.
new_statements.locator: Chapter 4 Prosody, §4.3 Word-level prosody, p. 124 (p. 155); disyllabic rule §4.3.1.1 p. 127; transcription note p. 75-76
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: The quotation was checked again. (888 pp., La Trobe thesis, text present). extracted text of p. 155 = book p. 124, §4.3 Word-level prosody, gives the passage exactly as quoted ("The metrical system is trochaic, that is, feet are left-headed.. Predicates carry the primary stress on the head of the rightmost (i.e. last) foot. Non-predicates carry the primary stress on the head of the leftmost (i.e. first) foot."); the only difference is the footnote marker 28 after "non-predicates", which the quote drops. Other locators also verified: p. 14 fn 5 (p. 45) "Tessmann's Nokaman is not included, since the data.. presents inconsistencies that require a special treatment that is beyond the scope of t…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Left-to-right disyllabic trochees. Non-predicates (nouns and all non-verbal citation forms) take primary stress on the first syllable; predicates (inflected verbs) take it on the head of the last foot (penult in even-syllabled words, antepenult in odd-syllabled ones, since degenerate feet are normally disallowed). Stress is realised as vowel lengthening. Independently, a high tone lands on the rightmost prominent syllable (the stressed one or a closed even-numbered syllable to its right; never word-final in 3+ syllable words), so the audible pitch peak is often not on the stressed syllable. p. 75: 'the duration stress falls on the first syllable in all the examples'. Stress is obligatory and culminative (p. 125).
new_statements.secondary_stress: The head of each non-primary foot carries secondary stress, realised as a vowel longer than in non-prominent syllables (§4.3.3, p. 136ff.); the third syllable of trisyllabic words carries none because degenerate feet are not formed (§4.3.2, p. 133).
new_statements.exceptions: Degenerate monosyllabic feet only under specific circumstances (§4.3.6); lexically assigned high tone in a few items (§4.3.9); monosyllables carry a phonetic rising pitch (§4.3.5); some phonological words in complex phrases lack a high tone entirely (§4.3.7); nominalised verbs count as non-predicates (fn 28). The author calls the whole account 'preliminary' (p. 121).
new_statements.domain_note: Phonological word; described for the Lower Aguaytía dialect of Kashibo-Kakataibo (p. 74), with only short recordings of Upper Aguaytía, Sungaroyacu and San Alejandro. The Nokamán (Pachitea) dialect itself is explicitly excluded from the thesis data (p. 14 fn 5). Stress = duration; tone = pitch; the two are distinguished throughout (Table 21, p. 126).
new_statements.identity_note: noca1240 is a retired code (Glottolog 'Bookkeeping'; ISO 639-3 CR 2022-016 merged [nom] into [cbr] on 2023-01-20). Nokamán is the extinct Pachitea-River dialect of Kashibo-Kakataibo (Cashibo-Cacataibo, cash1251), closest to the San Alejandro dialect (Zariquiey 2011b: 8-9; 2013). The quoted statement describes the Lower Aguaytía dialect of cash1251, not Nokamán, whose only data are Tessmann 1930's accented wordlist (accents on varying syllables: úni, nónti vs toná, kaná, pasí; Zariquiey 2013: 26 reads Tessmann's acute as marking 'stress/high tone'). by our rule that each source is filed under the language's current Glottolog code (a retired code does not make a separate language) this should be filed under cash1251, which is also on the target list with an empty scan, not as a separate noca1240 entry.

sources.locator: Chapter 4 Prosody, §4.3 Word-level prosody, p. 124 (p. 155); disyllabic rule §4.3.1.1 p. 127; transcription note p. 75-76
sources.note: Ch. 4 Prosody, §4.3 (p. 124): trochaic feet built left to right; primary stress (= vowel lengthening) on the head of the leftmost foot in non-predicates, on the head of the rightmost foot in predicates; secondary stress on other foot heads; separate weight-sensitive high tone on the rightmost prominent syllable. Describes the Lower Aguaytía dialect; Tessmann's Nokamán data explicitly excluded (p. 14 fn 5).

sources.citation: Zariquiey Biondi, Roberto. 2013. Tessmann's <Nokamán>: a linguistic investigation of a mysterious Panoan group. Cadernos de Etnolingüística 5(2): 1-48.
sources.note: §5 'Some phonological issues about <Nokamán>' covers segments only; sole prosody remark p. 26: 'the final n and the position of the stress/high tone on the last syllable (suggested by how Tessmann codified the name) remain unexplained'. Reproduces Tessmann 1930 pp. 184-187 in facsimile (appendix, paper pp. 31-33): Tessmann's acute accents fall on varying syllables (úni 'man', nónti 'canoe' vs toná 'black', kaná 'thunder', pasí 'red').
Nothing on stress; lists Nokamán as the extinct dialect closest to San Alejandro (citing Zariquiey 2018).

sources.citation: Fleck, David W. 2013. Panoan languages and linguistics. Anthropological Papers of the American Museum of Natural History 99.
sources.note: Lists Nokaman as a Kashibo dialect (classification p. 11; synonymy Kamano/Camano p. 85; sources p. 98: Tessmann 1930: 184-187, 228-word list + 139 terms). Notes contrastive tone only in Chakobo, Kapanawa, Amawaka (p. 51). No stress statement for Kashibo or Nokaman; drops all stress marks from ethnonyms 'due to the inconsistency with which these are applied'.
sources.venue: Anthropological Papers of the American Museum of Natural History 99

sources.citation: Zariquiey Biondi, Roberto. 2013. Del <Kaschibo> de Tessmann al cashibo-cacataibo contemporáneo: algunas notas para la comprensión de la historia lingüística de un pueblo pano. Revista Brasileira de Linguística Antropológica 5(1): 159-192.
sources.note: Comparative study of Tessmann's Kaschibo lists; treats Nokamán as a probably extinct fifth dialect closest to San Alejandro (p. 164). Nothing on stress.

sources.citation: Zariquiey, Roberto. 2011. Aproximación dialectológica a la lengua cashibo-cacataibo (pano). Lexis 35(1): 5-46.
sources.note: Segmental/lexical/morphosyntactic isoglosses of the four living dialects; identifies Nokamán with Wistrand's 'Camano' of the Pachitea and groups it with San Alejandro (pp. 8-9). Nothing on stress or accent.

sources.citation: Tessmann, Günter. 1930. Die Indianer Nordost-Perus: Grundlegende Forschungen für eine systematische Kulturkunde. Hamburg: Friederichsen, de Gruyter. pp. 172-187 (Nokamán sketch + 228-word list).
sources.note: Only the wordlist pages were seen (as facsimile images). Forms carry acute accents on varying syllables; no rule is stated on these pages. Tessmann's introductory note on what his accent marks mean was not reachable (full book not online: archive.org 0 hits, HathiTrust/Google Books/Zenon/HEIDI all bot-walled).
